evidence.reason: The finding is a proposal to add new protection machinery — a durable 'unresolved deployment intent' artifact consulted by both entrypoints (runbook and controller) under the controller lock and kept unresolved through health and recovery — not an implementation error in existing intended behavior. The module docstring documents the current design boundary explicitly: serialization is by advisory locks held during a live run ('the controller's own controller.lock is held for the same window... so a controller transaction cannot overlap the switches or the health window: controller transactions read neither deploy.lock nor the admission marker'), and process death is handled by the retained O_EXCL admission marker plus the pre-admission recovery receipt (persist_recovery_receipt, lines 768-771) that owner-run recovery reads (RecoveryRequired/exit 3). That the controller does not consult runbook state before a unit transaction, and that a second runbook can run after admission release, is the documented design, not an overlooked bug; no contract clause or stated intent requires blocking mutations between a runbook crash and recovery. The docstring also records that the owner retired the heavier deploy ceremony on 2026-11-14 (dogfooded alpha, kept properties enumerated: queue bytes never written, lock-serialized deploys, held admission, helper-fenced switch, measured rollback) — none of which is a cross-entrypoint deployment-intent fence. Hardening crash coordination across entrypoints enlarges protection scope in an owner deploy-trust area and does not itself establish a defect.
